claims.text: The NCSC says PHP published a security update for a critical issue that may allow attackers to execute commands on any web server running PHP.
The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and organisations using any version of PHP are affected.
An attacker could trigger an out-of-memory condition that results in memory corruption, which under certain conditions could be exploited for unauthenticated remote code execution.
The issue has been fixed. The NCSC advises identifying systems running PHP, prioritising internet-facing ones, and updating to the latest version.
If updating is not possible, the PHP Foundation has provided temporary mitigations; if those cannot be applied, the NCSC says to consider taking the system offline and to look for backdoors.
The NCSC alert does not use the name Black October, and does not report developer overtime or companies pulling websites down.

metadata.description: Running a PHP website? The UK's NCSC has issued an alert about a critical PHP issue (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that may allow attackers to execute commands on web servers. This video explains the risk, the fix, and what to do if you cannot update immediately. The name Black October is not used in the official alert.

Schools Higher education Professional skills training Working with the NCSC Research & academia Education & academia resources Cyber Skills Training resources for school staff Resources for higher education institutions Cyber Security Body of Knowledge (CyBOK) Industry & skill resources CYBERUK 2027 NCSC for StartUps Industry 100 Cyber League News Back News All the latest information to help you keep track of what's happening In this section News Blogs Speeches Reports & advisories Malware analysis reports CYBERUK 2027 Stay up to date The NCSC's Cyber Series podcast Subscribe About NCSC Report an incident Contact us Close Search Search Popular Searches Passkeys Training Cyber Essentials AI Phishing Cyber Assessment Framework News Download & print article PDF Download & print article PDF Critical security issue affecting PHP The NCSC is encouraging UK organisations to take immediate action to mitigate a security issue affecting PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). What has happened? PHP has published a security update to address a critical security issue that may allow attackers to execute commands on any web server running PHP. PHP (PHP Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely used server-side scripting language designed for web development. It runs on a web server to generate dynamic page content, interact with databases, and handle backend application logic before delivering the final HTML output to a user's browser. PHP is also used in a range of other products. The security issue could allow an attacker to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) condition in PHP that results in memory corruption. Under certain conditions, this corruption could be exploited to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. This security issue has now been fixed. CVE-2026-109618 : Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 : Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. The full PHP security advisory provides more details regarding the fixed security issue. The NCSC will continue to monitor for any impact on UK organisations. Who is affected? Organisations using any version of PHP are affected and all organisations are highly encouraged to update to the latest fixed version. Organisations using older versions of PHP are highly encouraged to update to a fully supported version. What should I do? The NCSC recommends following vendor best practice advice in the mitigation of vulnerabilities. The NCSC highly encourages organisations to follow these priority actions: Identify systems running PHP across your infrastructure, prioritising internet-facing systems. As all versions may be affected, do not limit discovery to outdated PHP versions; identify PHP installations generally and assess their exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Update to the latest version of PHP and continue to monitor for future updates. Prioritise internet-facing systems first and then internal systems. If you are unable to update to a version with the security update applied, the PHP Foundation have provided temporary mitigations . If you are unable to apply the temporary mitigations, or applying them would take too long, you should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated. If you are unable to update or disable the system immediately then you should assess the system for any evidence of compromise prior to your upgrade or mitigation and look for backdoors installed by an attacker. If you are not confident in your ability to do this yourselves then you can get assistance from an NCSC-assured Cyber Incident Response provider . Continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP. NCSC-NL have published an inventory list of software products with a PHP dependency potentially affected by the vulnerabilities. Apply relevant updates as they become available. script_sections.narration: Watch this if you run a PHP website, because a critical security flaw could let attackers run commands on your server.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre says the issue is tracked as two flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and it affects every version of PHP.

Here is how it works. An attacker can trigger an out-of-memory condition, which corrupts memory. Under certain conditions, that can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution, meaning no login is needed.
The good news is that PHP has released a fix. First, find every system running PHP, starting with the ones facing the internet. Then update to the latest version.
If you cannot update yet, the PHP Foundation has published temporary mitigations. If those are not possible either, the NCSC says to consider taking the system offline, and check it for backdoors.
Some people call this Black October, but the official alert does not use that name. Check your PHP version today.
